kp.k: Siloed infrastructure limits in-house lawyers' strategic contribution
kp.d: Drawing on procurement consulting experience, Strydom argues that in-house lawyers need commercial as well as legal reasoning. Legal teams receive requests after business discussions have already occurred, while their separate tooling deprives them of context needed to advise strategically rather than merely mitigate risk.
qs: in-house attorneys are truly these commercial strategists, enabling business growth more than risk mitigation.

kp.k: CLMs often store contracts without capturing working context
kp.d: Strydom reports that many large mining and logistics organizations he encountered did not use contract lifecycle management systems, while users often treated them primarily as repositories. Both speakers describe email and lawyers' personal knowledge as important context sources. These are practitioner observations, not quantified deployment findings.

the ones that did, it felt like they were very underutilized to a point where they were basically just being used as a source of truth.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Strydom claims AI is already improving lawyers' performance and predicts changes to in-house workflows, legal technology purchasing, institutional knowledge management and legal careers.
pts.d: Jarryd Strydom argues that connecting legal tooling to broader business context enables in-house lawyers to act as commercial strategic advisers while retaining risk mitigation responsibilities. He describes a shift from tools requiring substantial user input toward tools that work for users, which he associates with declining CLM usage. He claims AI has reached a point of practical usefulness and that lawyers using it perform better than those who do not. AI adoption elsewhere in businesses increases pressure on legal departments to match faster workflows. On build versus buy, he says personally built AI workflows can replicate some point-solution functionality, but predicts continuing demand for specialized vertical AI platforms where integration, organizational scale and institutional knowledge matter. He presents centralized knowledge systems as a way to retain expertise beyond individual employees and says AI makes playbooks easier to create, tailor and update using negotiation data. On careers, he predicts legal-tech recruitment will compete with law firms for graduates, while expressing concern about lost practical training. He also says AI can accelerate the transition from law school to practice and enable broader, more generalist legal knowledge.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw primarily on Strydom's professional experience, product-building experience and informal conversations with in-house legal teams, rather than reported comparative studies.
pts.d: Strydom cites experience as a private-practice and in-house lawyer, a programmer and a McKinsey consultant working on legal procurement. His observations about adoption, build-versus-buy decisions and team structure come mainly from a recent US road show, including California, Seattle and cities in Texas. He describes firsthand examples of underused CLMs, context stored in email and individual lawyers' private negotiation notes. His estimate that substantive AI awareness is above 50% is an impression offered in response to the interview question, without a sample size or survey methodology. Likewise, he supplies no measured performance comparison for his claim that AI users outperform nonusers, no usage series for CLM decline and no measured outcomes for playbook improvements. His claims about Sandstone's capabilities and the value of vertical platforms are those of its co-founder; the host discloses being an investor. The host's survey references and separate predictions are not treated as Strydom's independent evidence or claims.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Most claims concern changes already occurring at the time of the 2026 interview; longer-term predictions are conditional on scale, integration and opportunities for practical learning.
pts.d: Strydom describes a marked increase in in-house AI knowledge compared with the same time the previous year, and presents AI usefulness, experimentation and playbook improvements as current developments. He qualifies adoption by noting that busy lawyers may lack time to learn AI-assisted coding and that not everyone is trying Claude. He expects greater uptake of personally built workflows among smaller teams, whereas organizational complexity and the need to integrate systems and scale across a department support his prediction of a continuing market for specialized platforms. Knowledge capture depends on connecting relevant sources, including individual notes; a meeting note taker to capture voice context is under consideration rather than described as already deployed. His career predictions are prospective: he warns that bypassing junior-associate training could weaken practical expertise, while agreeing that AI could improve early-career learning. He explicitly projects a different lawyer knowledge base over the next ten years.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The main affected groups are corporate legal departments, their business colleagues, legal software providers, law firms and lawyers entering the profession.
pts.d: In-house lawyers are portrayed as gaining access to business context, stronger strategic-advisory capabilities and reusable institutional knowledge, while facing competitive and internal pressure to adopt AI. Smaller legal teams may build their own workflows; larger departments face integration, consistency and knowledge-retention requirements that Strydom says favor specialized platforms. Sales, IT and other business functions create faster demands on legal as they adopt AI themselves. CLM providers and narrow redlining software vendors face changing user expectations and potential replication of functionality through AI-assisted coding, while vertical platform providers such as Sandstone are presented as retaining a role at department scale. Strydom reports hearing interest in legal teams with more senior lawyers, fewer juniors and more systems-oriented working; this is a reported staffing preference, not a quantified finding of AI-driven job losses. Law firms may compete with legal-tech vendors such as Harvey and Legora for graduates. Students and junior lawyers gain alternative career paths and potential AI-supported learning, but may lose practical apprenticeship experience if they bypass practice.
